content: Evidence suggests that the safety and effectiveness of abortion care provided by midwives is supported with moderate certainty. Women often perceive care from midwives as more supportive compared to other healthcare providers, based on moderate-certainty evidence. However, women’s satisfaction with the overall abortion experience when midwives are involved is supported by low-certainty evidence. This approach has been shown to be feasible, even in low-resource settings. For associate and advanced associate clinicians, evidence supports the safety and effectiveness of their involvement in abortion care with moderate certainty. Women’s satisfaction with the overall abortion experience under their care is supported by low-certainty evidence. This option is feasible across all resource settings and may reduce inequities by extending quality abortion care to underserved populations. Generalist medical practitioners are recommended to provide abortion care within their typical scope of practice. No direct evidence was found comparing their safety and effectiveness to specialist medical practitioners. However, this option is feasible in both highand low-resource settings where dilation and evacuation (D&E) is commonly used. Generalist practitioners routinely perform other surgical procedures, such as cesarean sections and vacuum aspirations, and their involvement may increase equitable access to quality abortion care, especially in settings where specialist providers are not always available. Specialist medical practitioners are recommended to provide abortion care within their typical scope of practice. No additional evidence assessment was conducted for this group, as their role is well-established. The WHO updated its recommendations from 2015, reviewing evidence related to traditional and complementary medicine professionals, auxiliary nurses, and auxiliary nurse midwives using the GRADE methodology. Recommendations for traditional and complementary medicine professionals were upgraded from “suggest” to “recommend,” while recommendations for other health worker categories remained unchanged. Vacuum aspiration procedures, both manual (MVA) and electric (EVA), can be performed in primary care facilities on an outpatient basis. MVA is more commonly used earlier in pregnancy and in settings without stable electricity access. Dilatation and sharp curettage (D&C) should be replaced with MVA due to its lower risk profile and better outcomes. For surgical abortion at gestational ages ≥14 weeks, dilation and evacuation (D&E) is strongly recommended. The gestational age threshold was revised from “over 12 weeks” to “14 weeks and above” to align with updated guidance. D&E requires greater skills and training compared to vacuum aspiration, and health workers providing care at ≥12 weeks may require additional professional and mentoring support. Key human rights considerations emphasize that healthcare facilities, commodities, and services must be available, accessible, acceptable, and of good quality. Evidence-based, scientifically appropriate, and up-to-date care is essential. The use of D&C, which causes pain and suffering, is incompatible with human rights standards and should not be used for abortion care. Medical abortion involves the use of medications such as mifepristone and misoprostol, either in combination or as standalone regimens. Letrozole, a third-generation selective aromatase inhibitor, can also be used in combination with misoprostol for early gestational medical abortion. Letrozole suppresses estrogen levels, altering progesterone receptor concentrations and leading to pregnancy loss. Medical abortion is a process that occurs over several days and includes assessing eligibility, administering medications, and evaluating the outcome. Community health workers (CHWs) are recommended to facilitate all three subtasks of medical abortion (assessing eligibility, administering medications, and evaluating outcomes) with moderate-certainty evidence supporting their safety, effectiveness, and acceptability. Pharmacy workers are also recommended to provide medical abortion services, with indirect evidence supporting their feasibility when tools for eligibility and outcome assessment are available. Traditional and complementary medicine professionals are recommended to provide abortion care, with evidence supporting their safety, effectiveness, and women’s satisfaction with their services. Auxiliary nurses and auxiliary nurse midwives are recommended to provide abortion care, supported by moderate-certainty evidence for safety and effectiveness. Nurses and midwives are also recommended to provide abortion care, with moderate-certainty evidence supporting their safety, effectiveness, and women’s satisfaction with their services. These options are feasible and already implemented in several countries.
